hints: Start by picturing blood leaving the heart twice for two different destinations - one short loop to a gas exchange organ and one long loop to the rest of the body.
The loop to the lungs is named after the lungs, and the loop to the rest of the body is named after the body systems it supplies.
For the vein, remember deoxygenated blood from all body tissues drains into the right atrium through one very large vein with superior and inferior branches.
walkthrough:
The Two Loops of Double Circulation**
Mammals have blood pass through the heart twice in one complete circuit. One loop goes from the right side of the heart to the lungs and back to the left side. That is the pulmonary circulation - pulmonary means to do with the lungs.

The Body Loop and Return Vein**
The second loop goes from the left side of the heart to all body tissues and back to the right side. That is the systemic circulation - systemic means the whole body system. All its deoxygenated blood is collected and returned to the right atrium by the largest vein, the vena cava.
Final answer: pulmonary circulation; systemic circulation; vena cava (superior / inferior vena cava).

hints: Think of the size sequence on the way back to the heart - blood leaves tiny capillaries, enters a slightly larger thin-walled collecting vessel, then enters a true vein.
walkthrough:
Linking Capillaries to Veins**
In a closed system there are no gaps. On the arterial side arterioles feed capillaries. On the venous side the mirror image happens - capillaries drain into small collecting vessels called venules, which then join to form veins that carry blood back toward the heart.

hints: First orientate Fig. 1.1 - remember the right side of the heart is on the left side of the diagram as you look at it, and find the large arching vessel leaving the ventricles toward the lungs.

Next think which atrioventricular valve must shut to stop backflow when the ventricle on the lung-circuit side contracts - it sits between right atrium and right ventricle with chordae tendinae attached.
walkthrough:
Finding the Artery to the Lungs**
Only the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Its outflow vessel curves up and splits left and right toward each lung. That is the pulmonary artery. It is unusual because it is an artery carrying deoxygenated blood, but artery simply means away from the heart. Label this L.

Finding the Valve That Closes in Right Ventricular Systole**
When the right ventricle contracts (systole), pressure rises and would push blood back into the right atrium. The right atrioventricular valve, with three cusps so also called the tricuspid valve, slams shut, held by chordae tendinae to prevent inversion. It lies between right atrium above and right ventricle below. Label this R, with the line touching the valve flaps themselves.
Final answer: L - label line to pulmonary artery (vessel from right ventricle to lungs); R - label line to right atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve between right atrium and right ventricle.

hints: Start with protein shape - enzymes that are compact, soluble and work in cytoplasm or blood plasma have a rounded 3-D shape, unlike strong rope-like structural proteins.
Think about location words - if carbonic anhydrase works inside the red blood cell cytoplasm, what prefix means inside the cell?
Recall what small molecule is always abundant inside cells and combines with $CO_2$ in the first step of this reaction.
The product with formula $H_2CO_3$ is a weak acid named after carbonate - think what $CO_2$ dissolved in water forms.
Finally, remember $H_2CO_3$ splits into two ions - one is $HCO_3^-$ given in the question, so the other must be the positively charged ion from an acid.
walkthrough:
Describing Carbonic Anhydrase**
Enzymes are soluble, roughly spherical proteins with a precise active site. That shape class is globular. Because this enzyme works in the cytoplasm of the red blood cell, not secreted outside, it is intracellular.

The Catalysed Reaction in Tissues**
In respiring tissues $CO_2$ diffuses into red blood cells. Carbonic anhydrase catalyses: $CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2CO_3$. So water combines with carbon dioxide to make carbonic acid.

Dissociation to Ions for Transport**
Carbonic acid then rapidly dissociates: $H_2CO_3 \rightarrow H^+ + HCO_3^-$. The hydrogen ions ($H^+$) bind to haemoglobin, and the hydrogencarbonate ions ($HCO_3^-$) diffuse out into the plasma for transport to the lungs. That is how most $CO_2$ is carried.
Final answer: globular protein; intracellular enzyme; water ($H_2O$) combined with $CO_2$ to form carbonic acid ($H_2CO_3$), which forms hydrogen ions ($H^+$) and hydrogencarbonate ions ($HCO_3^-$).
